prime.problem: GPT-2 needs a table to turn token ids into vectors at the bottom and a layer to turn its final vector into 50,257 scores at the top. Built separately, those are two 50,257 × 768 matrices: almost a third of the model spent twice on the same tokens.
prime.fits: You have the full GPT module and a loss that falls. This card revisits the embedding lookup from the MLP course and the output layer you wrote in the module card, and notices they are the same shape.
prime.goal: Explain why one matrix can do both jobs, add the one-line tie to your model, and predict how it changes the parameter count and which rows get gradients.

attend: Why do nn.Embedding(50257, 768) and nn.Linear(768, 50257) end up with exactly the same weight shape?
What does row i do at the bottom of the model, and what does the same row do at the top?
Why would a row that is close to ' queen' help at both ends at once?
Which rows of an untied wte get no gradient in a batch, and how does tying change that?
How would you prove the two names share memory rather than just holding equal values?

must: nn.Linear stores its weight as (out, in) = (50257, 768) → the same shape as the embedding table → row i is token i in both → one tensor can serve as input lookup and output scorer

Similar tokens should have close rows at the input and get similar scores at the output → sharing one matrix makes both true together → each update to a row improves how the token is read and how it is predicted

Assigning the Parameter (not copying values) → both modules point at one memory block → the gradient is the sum of both uses → every row trains every step through the softmax, not only the rows of tokens in the batch
The table is 50,257 × 768 = 38.6M numbers → 31% of the 124M model → tying cuts the count from 163.0M to 124.4M → the saving shrinks as the width grows relative to the vocabulary
elevated: state_dict() still lists both names (149 entries, 148 parameters) → summing it double-counts to 163,037,184 → count with model.parameters(), which lists a shared tensor once
reference: the tie line: self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight (train_gpt2.py L93–L94, commit ec39245)
tensor.data_ptr() returns the memory address; equal addresses mean the same storage
_init_weights reaches the shared tensor twice (as Linear and as Embedding), both with std 0.02

compress.prompt: From memory, draw GPT-2 as a column with the shared matrix W beside it. Mark where W is used as a lookup and where as a dot product, and write the parameter arithmetic next to it.
checklist: bottom: x = W[i], take token i's row
top: logits = h · W[j] for every token j, 50,257 scores
why: similar tokens → close rows → similar input vectors and similar scores
one tensor, so gradients from both uses add up

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words why the input embedding and the output layer can reasonably be the same matrix, rather than two that happen to have the same shape.
answer: each row stands for one token in both places
a good row puts similar tokens close together
that closeness helps both reading a token in and scoring it as the next token
sharing forces the two roles to agree

retrieve.q: Walk through one training step with tying on: which forward operations touch W, and what happens to W's gradient before the optimizer step?
answer: forward: wte gathers the rows of the input tokens
forward: lm_head takes a dot product with every row
backward: the lookup sends gradient to the rows used; the output layer sends gradient to all rows
both contributions are added into the one W.grad; the optimizer updates W once

retrieve.q: You copy the values with wte.weight.data = lm_head.weight.data.clone() instead of assigning the Parameter. What do you gain, what do you lose, and how would you catch the mistake?
answer: they are equal only at the start and drift apart after the first step
no parameter saving: still 163,037,184
memory is still doubled
catch it: data_ptr() differs, or the parameter count doesn't drop

retrieve.q: Why does tying save 31% of GPT-2 124M but only about 5% of GPT-2's largest 1,542M model?
answer: the table is vocab × width: 50,257 × 768 vs 50,257 × 1,600
the blocks grow much faster with width and depth than the table does
so the table's share of the model falls as models grow

compare.q: The MLP course's C[X] table and GPT-2's tied wte both turn ids into vectors. What is fundamentally different about how their rows are trained, and which design choice causes it?
answer: C is only read at the input, so a row learns only when its character appears in the batch
the tied wte is also the output layer, so every row gets gradient every step
cause: sharing the matrix with the softmax output
with 27 characters the difference barely matters; with 50,257 tokens many are rare, so it matters

compare.q: In micrograd, a used twice needs += in backward. How is a tied W the same situation, and what would go wrong if PyTorch overwrote instead of adding?
answer: W is one leaf used by two operations, just like a in a + a
its gradient must be the sum of both paths
overwriting would keep only one use's gradient, so W would learn as only an embedding or only an output layer

compare.q: Padding the vocabulary to 50,304 adds 47 tokens that never appear in the data. How does tying interact with that padding: what does it cost and how are those rows trained?
answer: the tied table grows by 47 × 768 = 36,096 parameters, counted once
the fake tokens never appear as inputs, so only the output side touches their rows
the softmax gives them a little probability, so each step pushes their scores down

predict.q: After padding to vocab 50,304, the 47 fake tokens never appear in the input or as targets. With tying on, will their rows of W ever get a nonzero gradient? And how many parameters does tying save now?
predict.answer: Yes, every step. The output layer scores every row, and the softmax gives each fake token a small probability, so the loss pushes those scores down through their rows. Tying now saves 50,304 × 768 = 38,633,472 parameters (computed: untied 163,109,376 vs tied 124,475,904).

apply.task: In your scratch copy of the lab, build GPT(GPTConfig()) and GPT(GPTConfig(tie=False)) with torch.manual_seed(1337), run one forward and backward on the first B=4, T=32 batch of tiny shakespeare, and count the rows of wte.weight.grad that are not all zero. Then count the distinct token ids in x.
apply.done: Untied: 67 rows have a gradient, the same as the 67 distinct tokens in x. Tied: all 50,257 rows do.
apply.hint: (g.abs().sum(1) > 0).sum() counts nonzero rows; x.unique().numel() counts distinct tokens.
